title: Reading the Validation Flow
body: Validation is the process of verifying whether code or data meets the expected conditions.
detail: Validation code is typically read in the following order: input verification, rule checking, collection of failed items, and output of results. Its role is not simply to check for errors, but to catch conditions in advance—such as missing fields, incorrect data types, duplicate IDs, and out-of-range values—that could cause the app to malfunction later on. In educational apps, it is crucial for automatically verifying quality criteria such as the number of cards, JSON structure, inclusion of correct answers, and side card connections.
examples: Check that the card JSON contains all of the following: id, question, choices, and answer.
If the "answer" is not found in the "choices," it is treated as a validation failure.

title: Understanding the Debugging Flow
body: Debugging is the process of narrowing down the reasons why code behaves differently than expected.
detail: When debugging, rather than fixing the issue immediately based solely on the symptoms, check the following in order: the conditions under which the error occurs, the error message, any suspicious input values, and finally, the point where the program last behaved normally. For a traceback, start by looking at the error type and message on the last line, then trace back up the file name and line numbers. It’s a good idea to use `print` or `logging` to check intermediate values, and after making a fix, leave a small verification command to ensure the same problem doesn’t occur again.
examples: If a KeyError occurs, first check to see if you tried to access a key that doesn't exist.
If a value seems unusual, check both the data type and the actual value using `print(type(x), x)`.

title: Reading JSON Data Streams
body: JSON is a text-based data format commonly used for storing or exchanging settings, card data, and API responses.
detail: When working with JSON code, you should distinguish between the string stage and the data structure stage after parsing. Data read from a file is initially a string, but after passing through `json.loads` or `json.load`, it becomes a dictionary or a list. After that, you can retrieve the necessary values using keys, indices, or loops. In practice, you can reduce errors by checking for encoding issues, missing keys, nested structures in lists and dictionaries, and the `ensure_ascii` option when saving data.
examples: `json.loads(text)` converts a JSON string into a Python dictionary or list.
json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False) is often used to save data without garbling Korean characters.

title: Reading the Pipeline Flow
body: A pipeline is a workflow consisting of multiple processing steps linked together in a specific order.
detail: It’s easier to understand pipeline code if you break it down into stages: receiving input, preprocessing, transforming, validating, and saving the results. Each stage takes the output from the previous stage as its input. Therefore, you need to check the filenames, intermediate outputs, restart points in case of failure, and logs together. In batch processing, it is also important to determine whether items that have already been processed are skipped and whether only failed items can be rerun.
examples: Data is processed in the following order: collection → refinement → validation → storage.
If you save the intermediate JSONL file, it will be easy to resume from that step in case of a failure.

title: Understanding the API Call Flow
body: An API is a standardized channel through which programs exchange data with other services.
detail: When reading API code, examine the request URL, method, headers, parameters or body, timeout, and response status code in that order. Even if a response appears to be successful, it’s safer to check the status code before parsing the JSON. Secrets, such as API keys, should not be hard-coded but should be read from environment variables. Since external calls can fail, be sure to also check for exception handling and retry limits.
examples: Set a timeout as shown in `requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)`.
After calling `response.raise_for_status()`, read the data using `response.json()`.

title: Reading the Database Code Flow
body: Database code deals with the structure for storing and retrieving data.
detail: Database-related code should be read in the following order: connection setup, table structure, queries, and result handling. CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, and Delete, and most data storage functions combine these four operations. When writing SQL directly, concatenating input values as strings can be risky, so you must verify parameter binding. In the app architecture, the repository layer serves to centralize database access.
examples: SELECT retrieves data, and INSERT adds new data.
The Repository pattern wraps database queries so that the app code doesn't have to worry as much about how data is stored.

title: Reading Schemas and Data Structures
body: A schema is a set of rules that define which fields and data types the data must have.
detail: By looking at the schema, you can first understand the structure of the data. You can determine which fields are required, whether they are strings or numbers, whether they are lists or dictionaries, and whether there are any value ranges. JSON objects, API responses, and database tables can all be analyzed from a schema perspective. When the schema is clear, it’s easier to automate validation, and even as the dataset grows, you can quickly identify missing values, typos, and type errors.
examples: A lesson card requires fields such as id, question, choices, and answer.
You can define data types such as `score` (a number) and `tags` (a list of strings).

title: Performance Bottlenecks in Reading
body: Performance is a measure of how fast and reliably code runs.
detail: Performance issues typically arise from the number of iterations, the number of file or network calls, redundant calculations, and how large datasets are processed. First, time each step to identify which ones are slow, and check whether the same data is being read repeatedly or the same API is being called over and over. Caching is a method of reusing the same results to reduce both processing time and costs. In batch processing, you must also consider the number of items to process at once and the cost of retrying in case of failure.
examples: Reading the same file repeatedly within a loop can slow things down.
Caching frequently used API responses can reduce the number of calls and lower costs.
